notes.meaning: Paul writes from prison because of his service to Jesus, urging believers to live in a way that matches what God called them to be. God has lavished great spiritual blessings on his people, so their everyday lives should reflect his goodness. Our daily conduct should bring honor to the Lord who saved us.

Christians are called to live with humility, gentleness, and patience toward one another. Humility means not thinking too highly of ourselves, while gentleness keeps us from becoming easily irritated. Because God bears with our faults, we must choose to put up with the weaknesses of others in love.

Believers must work hard to guard the harmony that the Holy Spirit has already created among them. Peace acts like a strong cord that ties very different people together into one family. God gives this unity as a gift, and our task is to protect it by refusing to let selfish quarrels tear it apart.

All believers make up one spiritual body, the church, and share the one Holy Spirit who gives them new life. They also share the same confident hope of living forever with God in heaven. Because they share one life and one future, they ought to share one heart.

The church has only one Master, Jesus Christ, who rules over all his people. There is only one true gospel faith in him, and one baptism by which believers are publicly joined to his family. These common bonds unite all Christians across every earthly difference.

differ.view: The one baptism is water baptism by immersion, given only to believers who make a personal profession of faith in Christ.
The one baptism is the Holy Spirit's work uniting the believer to Christ, symbolized by water baptism which should never be repeated even if received in infancy.
The verse speaks of water baptism as the outward sign of salvation shared by all Christians, which does not rule out a distinct baptism in the Holy Spirit later on.

notes.meaning: There is only one God, the Father of all believers, who rules supreme above all creation. His power works through all things, and his Spirit lives inside every Christian heart. Having the same heavenly Father makes all believers true brothers and sisters.

While all Christians share the same salvation, Christ gives different spiritual gifts to each believer. No person receives every gift, and no one is left with nothing. Each member receives just what Christ chooses to give for the good of the whole church.

Paul quotes Psalm 68 to describe Jesus as a conquering King ascending to heaven. In ancient times, a victorious ruler marched his captured enemies through the city and gave gifts from the victory to his people. In the same way, Jesus defeated sin and death and poured out spiritual gifts on his church.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The original Hebrew text of Psalm 68 says the conqueror received gifts among men, and Paul either adapted the wording or used a familiar interpretive tradition to highlight Christ's generous giving.

notes.meaning: Before Jesus went up to heaven as victor, he first stepped down to earth in great humility. He took on human flesh, lived among us, died, and was buried. Now he is raised high above the heavens so that his divine presence and authority might fill the entire universe.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The lower parts of the earth refer not only to the grave, but to the underworld of departed souls where Christ went after his death to proclaim redemption before his resurrection.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars debate whether the descent refers to the incarnation on earth, a descent into the realm of the dead between death and resurrection, or the descent of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost.

notes.meaning: The ascended Christ gave gifted leaders to guide his church. He gave apostles to plant churches, prophets to speak God's messages, evangelists to preach the good news, and pastors and teachers to shepherd and teach local flocks. These leaders are themselves Christ's gifts to his people.

differ.view: Offices like apostles and prophets were temporary and foundational for the early church, while pastors and teachers are the continuing offices meant for every generation.
While the original revelatory apostles were unique to the founding era, apostolic and prophetic functions should continue to operate in the church today.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some teach that all five ministry offices, including modern apostles and prophets, must be restored today for the church to reach its full spiritual maturity.

notes.meaning: Church leaders are not appointed to do all the work of ministry by themselves. Their primary job is to train and equip God's people so that all believers can serve and care for one another. As every member serves, the whole body of Christ grows stronger.

Christian teaching and service must continue until all believers are united in the faith and truly know the Son of God. The goal is for the whole church to grow out of spiritual childhood into full maturity. Christ himself is the standard of complete spiritual health that we are growing toward.

God wants his people to stop acting like helpless infants in their spiritual understanding. Small boats without rudders get tossed around by rough waves, and unsteady Christians can be blown off course by every new teaching. Clever deceivers often use crafty tricks, like dishonest gamblers rolling loaded dice, to lead believers into error.

Instead of being tricked by lies, believers must hold firmly to God's truth and share it in genuine love. Truth without love becomes harsh, while love without truth quickly compromises with error. When we join truth and love together, we grow up in every part of our lives to be more like Christ, who is our head.

Christ provides life and direction to the whole church, just as a head directs a human body. Every member and supporting joint has a necessary part to play in supplying strength and nourishment to the others. When each part works properly, the entire body grows and builds itself up in love.

Paul urges believers with the authority of the Lord to leave behind their old pagan way of living. Unbelievers spend their lives chasing empty and worthless goals that cannot satisfy the soul. Christians have been rescued from that foolishness and must think and live differently.

People who do not know God live with darkened minds and are cut off from the spiritual life he offers. This separation happens because they are ignorant of God's truth and have stubbornly hardened their hearts against him. When the heart becomes calloused toward God, the mind loses the ability to recognize what is right.

When people repeatedly silence their consciences, they lose all sense of shame or pain over doing wrong. They end up throwing themselves into wild lust and every kind of impure behavior. Sin never satisfies them, so they constantly crave more self-indulgence.

That shameless and immoral lifestyle is the exact opposite of what it means to know Christ. Learning Christ is not just about memorizing facts; it means being transformed by his holy character. Those who truly belong to him cannot keep living in deliberate sin.

Paul knows his readers have heard Jesus speak to their hearts and have been taught by him. The real truth about God and human life is fully revealed in Jesus, both in what he said and how he lived. Following his truth requires turning away from worldly deceit.

Believers are commanded to take off their old, sinful nature just like throwing away dirty, ruined clothing. That old way of life was ruled by deceitful cravings that promised joy but only brought spiritual decay and misery. Becoming a Christian requires an active choice to leave those former habits behind.

Christians must allow their deepest thoughts and attitudes to be made fresh and new. Modifying outward habits is not enough; the Holy Spirit must renew the inner mind day by day. This spiritual makeover helps believers desire what honors God.

Believers must put on the new self, like putting on clean, holy garments. God creates this new nature to be like him, marked by genuine righteousness toward others and true holiness toward God. It restores the image of God that was broken by human sin.

Because believers are made new, they must stop lying and speak honestly to their neighbors. All Christians are connected to one another like limbs on the same body. Just as the hand would never deceive the eye, Christians must be honest so they do not destroy trust in the church.

When feelings of anger arise, believers must take care not to let them turn into sinful malice or revenge. Anger should be dealt with quickly before night falls, rather than being allowed to smolder into resentment. Holding onto a grudge gives the devil a foothold to stir up strife and ruin relationships.

Anyone who used to steal must stop taking what belongs to others and begin doing honest work with their own hands. God calls people to work not only to support themselves, but to have surplus to share with the poor. God changes a person from being a selfish taker into a generous giver.

Christians must avoid using foul, rotten, or cutting words that hurt other people. Instead, our speech should fit the situation and build others up in their faith. Encouraging words become a channel of God's grace to help those who hear them.

Believers must not bring sorrow to the Holy Spirit by clinging to unholy thoughts, foul speech, or bad tempers. The Spirit is God's seal placed upon believers to mark them as his own until the day their bodies are redeemed from the grave. Grieving the Spirit dampens our joy and harms our close walk with God.

Paul commands the church to sweep away all inner bitterness, sudden temper tantrums, and lasting resentments. He also forbids loud shouting matches, insulting words, and every cruel desire to hurt someone else. These harmful habits belong to the old life and have no place in God's family.

Instead of harboring anger, believers must treat one another with kindness, sympathy, and a willingness to forgive. We must forgive others freely and completely, because God has already forgiven our sins through Christ. God's immense mercy toward us is the model and the reason for how we forgive each other.
